text: When you add up the families pushed out by the full plan, it comes to about four thousand.
Four thousand households told to find somewhere else to live.

The plan moved through public hearings and a thick official report, all of it carrying the language of conservation and improvement, while the people whose homes were on the list had little say in whether they stayed.
The university did not do this on credit alone.

Kimpton said the university put in twenty-nine million dollars of its own money to buy, control, and rebuild the land, and that university money helped unlock far larger sums, federal grants and a quarter of a billion dollars in private investment.
This was the most expensive thing the university had ever done that wasn't a building with its name on it.
The promise, the thing everyone repeated, was a stable, integrated neighborhood, an example for all, what supporters called a compatible community.
And on the surface, Hyde Park did stay integrated, which set it apart from almost every other neighborhood near a changing South Side.
But look at who actually got to come back, and the picture turns.
Two sociologists, Peter Rossi and Robert Dentler, studied the renewal up close and published their findings in 1961 in a book called The Politics of Urban Renewal.
Their numbers are the ones that last.
In the first projects, Hyde Park A and B, about forty-six percent of the white families who lost their homes relocated somewhere else inside Hyde Park and Kenwood.
Among the Black families who lost their homes, it was about seventeen percent.
Same neighborhood, same clearance, two completely different outcomes.
The reason was money, and it was built into the plan.
The new buildings that replaced the cleared blocks were expensive.
The cheap rooms were gone on purpose, because the cheap rooms were what the plan defined as blight.
So the people who could afford the new Hyde Park stayed, and the people who couldn't were scattered to the South and West Sides, into neighborhoods that were themselves getting more crowded.
